record.title: Loopjacking paper reports agent approval reused for materially changed operations in tested product paths
record.summary: A September 2026 preprint defines Loopjacking as product logic applying a human decision for an operation A to a materially different operation B. In purposively selected tests, the author reports post-approval substitution in seven sampled Agno AgentOS releases and 12 sampled in-memory LangGraph Agent Server compositions with a declared authorization policy, plus an incomplete shell-command approval representation in OpenClaw 2026.2.23. OpenClaw 2026.2.24 rejected the tested mismatch. OpenAI Agents SDK 0.22.0 and 0.22.2 served as negative controls that rejected same-call mutation. The tests used synthetic principals and harmless recording sinks; they do not estimate prevalence, establish user susceptibility, or show all versions are affected.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper defines Loopjacking as product-owned logic using a human decision understood as approval for operation A to authorize or release a materially different operation B, and separates incomplete representation before approval from state substitution after approval.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The author reports reproducing post-approval substitution in seven sampled Agno AgentOS releases (2.5.6, 2.9.0, 3.0.1, 3.0.2, 3.0.3, 3.0.6, 3.0.9) and 12 sampled LangGraph Agent Server versions from 0.7.5 through 0.14.0 in a specified in-memory composition with a custom authorization policy.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The author reports that OpenClaw 2026.2.23 released a shell-command vector whose approval view omitted materially different arguments, while 2026.2.24 rejected the tested mismatch; the 0.22.0 and 0.22.2 OpenAI Agents SDK negative controls rejected same-call-ID mutation and executed unchanged approved calls.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the tested traces, exact use-time comparison or a policy denying unauthorized pending-state updates blocked the substituted operation while preserving execution of the unchanged approved operation.

contradictory_evidence: The tested set was purposive and does not estimate ecosystem prevalence or establish an uninterrupted affected-version range.
The LangGraph result depends on a declared custom authorization policy and in-memory composition; production Postgres was not evaluated.
OpenClaw 2026.2.24 rejected the tested representation mismatch; the paper states that the approval role was scripted, so human comprehension or deception rates were not tested.
OpenAI Agents SDK 0.22.0 and 0.22.2 rejected mutation in the tested ordinary per-call approval path, showing that continuation and serialization alone are not sufficient causes.

evidence_gaps.description: Independent execution of the archived Agno, LangGraph, OpenClaw, and OpenAI negative-control bundles has not been performed in this activation.
No comprehensive current affected-version map or prevalence estimate is established; the paper's release evidence cutoff is September 10, 2026.

brief.importance_rationale: If approval-to-execution mismatches occur in deployed agent workflows, they can let a lower-privilege actor reuse a human decision to authorize a different consequential action. The paper reports narrowly scoped product-path traces and fixes or controls; purposive testing does not estimate prevalence or affected-market size.
limitations: The preprint reports one researcher's controlled tests; the research desk did not independently reproduce them or execute the archive verifier.
The evidence cutoff is September 10, 2026. Exact tested releases are reported; later versions and deployments are not classified.
Agno and LangGraph have no vendor-fixed release established in the inspected archive. The LangGraph result is conditional on the tested in-memory composition and authorization policy.
Synthetic credentials and harmless recording sinks establish the tested operation dispatched by the product but do not show real funds, production data, or customer systems were affected.
The OpenClaw approval role was scripted after observing the product event; the study does not measure human comprehension or interface deception.
brief.summary: A September 2026 preprint defines Loopjacking as product logic applying a human decision for an operation A to a materially different operation B. In purposively selected tests, the author reports post-approval substitution in seven sampled Agno AgentOS releases and 12 sampled in-memory LangGraph Agent Server compositions with a declared authorization policy, plus an incomplete shell-command approval representation in OpenClaw 2026.2.23. OpenClaw 2026.2.24 rejected the tested mismatch. OpenAI Agents SDK 0.22.0 and 0.22.2 served as negative controls that rejected same-call mutation. technical.claimed_result: The author reports controlled native traces in three distinct product paths, with an OpenAI Agents SDK negative control, and shows tested defenses that block the mismatch while preserving unchanged A.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary sources establish what the paper and archive report, including exact versions, conditional configuration, synthetic sinks, and controls. the research desk has not independently run the archive or verified the reported executions.
technical.mechanism: A human reviews a rendered or canonical operation A; later product logic consumes the approval for current operation B without a comparison of the complete material effect, target, principal, task and scope. The paper distinguishes B already hidden or incomplete at review time from B substituted after review.
technical.regime: Purposively selected released versions tested through local product paths with synthetic principals, deterministic local models, loopback services, and harmless append-only ledgers or temporary files. LangGraph used an in-memory Agent Server composition and a declared authorization policy. Evidence cutoff 2026-09-10.
technical.reproducibility: A public archive lists checksummed evidence bundles and a Python verifier. This activation inspected the repository README and inventory only; it did not execute the verifier or reproduce any harness.
technical.strongest_baseline: Unchanged approved A execution, direct unapproved B denial, actor/session boundary controls, the OpenAI Agents SDK negative control, OpenClaw's 2026.2.24 fixed behavior, and a research exact-action comparison or deny-update policy.

brief.title: Loopjacking paper reports agent approval reused for materially changed operations in tested product paths
brief.why_it_matters: If these traces generalize to deployed approval workflows, a visible approval can fail to constrain what an agent ultimately executes. Reconstructing the complete operation and comparing it at use time, or preventing unauthorized changes to pending state, gives implementers a testable security invariant.
